title: Why do we mind our Ps and Qs? | PRINTING TERMS

entries.note: [[see:Gutenberg]]'s press made printing far more efficient, with reusable pieces and oil-based ink, though [[see:Bi Sheng]] developed movable type centuries earlier.
Credited with the printing press; his reusable type pieces and oil-based ink raised output from about 50 to 4,000 pages a day.
A system using wood or metal blocks to stamp letters on paper, first developed by Chinese inventor [[see:Bi Sheng]].
Chinese inventor who developed the first known [[see:movable type]] system some 400 to 500 years before [[see:Gutenberg]].
Produced the first English-language books and set up Britain's first printing works in London, bringing in continental printers to run his presses.

entries.term: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
entries.note: The first book [[see:William Caxton]] printed in English, around 1474, a translation from French of stories about Troy.
Caxton's anglicised form of French [[from:recueil]], a collection, made because he couldn't think of a good English translation.
A colloquial name for a printed book at the time, after the influential printer [[from:William Caxton]].
Had no H until Flemish printers added one, probably because their own word [[see:gheest]] had an H.
Words like [[see:where]] and [[see:what]] were originally spelled hw; printers switched them to wh to match ch, th and sh.
An example of a word originally spelled hw, whose spelling printers changed to [[see:wh]].
An example of a word originally spelled hw, whose spelling printers changed to [[see:wh]].
Printers added its silent B to match words like [[see:comb]] that already had one.
Already had a silent B, which printers copied onto [[see:thumb]].
Printers added a silent L to match [[see:would]] and [[see:should]], although [[from:can]] has no L.
Has a grammatically justified L from [[from:will]], which printers copied into [[see:could]].
Has a grammatically justified L from [[from:shall]], which printers copied into [[see:could]].
An ink-covered boy who did a print shop's drudge work; perhaps a joke on his blackened look, or a jab from hand copyists.
The taut fabric that holds the paper ready for printing.
The plate in a letterpress that presses the paper against the type.
Where worn-out and broken type was thrown, for the [[see:printer's devil]] to sort through.
Another name sometimes given to [[see:printer's devil]]s, the little urchins doing the drudge work.
A warning to novice typesetters not to confuse the similar, reversed p and q [[see:sorts]]; a rival theory derives it from 'please and thank yous'.
The small individual pieces of type laid out in reverse to make up a page.
What compositors called the pressmen, so the printing room was the [[see:pigsty]].
Compositors' name for the printing room, since they called the printers [[see:pigs]].
The patron devil of printing, blamed for scribes' errors from the 13th century and later for typos in print shops, like 1631's 'Thou shalt commit adultery'.
A printed sheet ruined by errors.
Financier of [[see:Gutenberg]]'s early presses; his name's similarity to [[see:Faust]] led to accusations of being in league with the devil.
Its similarity to [[see:Johann Fust]]'s name fed superstitions that printing was devilish.
Magic spells are so called because they are spelled out, linking writing and witchcraft.
Originally a French past participle imitating the sound of casting type; part of [[see:stereotype]] printing.
A metal plate of a whole page for reprinting; in 1922 [[see:Walter Lippmann]] applied it to oversimplified mental pictures of groups.
American publisher that should have ordered [[see:stereotype]]s for [[see:The Scarlet Letter]] after it sold out its 2,500-copy run.
Hawthorne's first novel, so popular a second run was needed after its type had been broken up, showing why [[see:stereotype]]s mattered.
The frame holding type blocks in the shape of a page.
A full page of type assembled in a [[see:chase]], which is why we still speak of filling out a form.
Media figure who in 1922 applied [[see:stereotype]] to rigid, repeated mental pictures of groups.
Has a printing origin very similar to [[see:stereotype]].
Capital letters were stored in the upper type case, so strictly it applies only to printed text, not handwriting.
Small letters were stored in the lower type case; the earlier terms were [[see:majuscule]] and [[see:minuscule]].
The word for capital letters before [[see:uppercase]], still the right term for handwriting.
The word for small letters before [[see:lowercase]], still the right term for handwriting.
So called because it stands at the head of a word or sentence.
The key that literally shifted a typewriter's [[see:carriage]] up so capitals lined up with the ribbon.
The part of a typewriter that carries the paper from side to side.
Keyboard key named for returning the typewriter [[see:carriage]] to the start of the line.
A later key that gives another key an alternative use.
Named because it let users enter control characters, control information rather than text, on old terminals.
From the 1680s, from Old French [[from:fondre]], to pour or melt, via type founding; a full set of type in one size and weight.
The businesses that cast molten metal into type, a process called type founding.
Shares its melting source with [[same-root:font]].
Despite the pouring connection, it doesn't share a root with [[unrelated:font]].
Doesn't share a root with [[unrelated:font]], despite appearances.
The spelling the 1888 printers' vocabulary uses throughout instead of [[see:font]].
The overall style of a character design, unlike a [[see:font]]; literally the face of the type block that makes the impression.
A typographic unit of 1/72 of an inch.
A typographic unit of a sixth of an inch; Latin pica means magpie, related to [[same-root:piebald]].
Historically short for magpie and, like [[same-root:pica]], used of jumbled things, including a jumble of type.
Describes magpie-like mixed colouring on an animal; related to [[same-root:pica]].
Originally meant not having enough [[see:sorts]] in a [[see:font]] to complete your page.
From Greek [[from:typos]], figure, image or form but also a blow; the verb comes from the noun.
Short for [[from:logotype]], from Greek logos, word, so the [[see:Apple logo]] technically isn't a logo but the [[see:Google logo]] is.
A single cast piece carrying several letters or a whole word, useful for repeated brand names.
Not technically a [[see:logo]] because it's not a word; the original was elaborate, showing Newton under a tree with words.
A true [[see:logo]] because it is a word.
An 1884 machine casting whole lines of type in hot metal, invented by [[see:Ottmar Mergenthaler]]; an American trademark short for 'line of type'.
Inventor of the [[see:Linotype]] machine.
Spacing between letters; originally the part of a type piece projecting beyond its body, from Old French [[from:carne]], projecting angle or hinge.
Spacing across an entire line, as opposed to [[see:kerning]].
Space between lines of text, from the thin strips of lead placed between lines of metal type.
A character joining two letters, like fi, from Latin [[from:ligare]], to bind; related to [[same-root:alloy]], [[same-root:ally]], [[same-root:liaison]], [[same-root:religion]].
Discussed in an earlier episode; an example of a [[see:ligature]], combining the letters of Latin et.
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Related to [[same-root:ligature]].
Slanted sorts that can overlap, named after Italy because [[see:Aldus Manutius]] introduced them in Venice in 1501; based on right-handed handwriting.
Introduced [[see:italic]] type in Venice in 1501.
The original name for [[see:italic]] type, after [[see:Aldus Manutius]].
Left-leaning [[see:italic]]s with no real use, suggested in previous episodes as a way to mark sarcasm.
An embellishment connecting letters in a [[see:ligature]] that isn't part of either letter; no link found with [[see:gadzooks]].
A cry of alarm or delight, probably short for [[from?:God's hooks]], the nails of the cross, or possibly God's hawks.
A typographic flourish.
A connecting stroke giving characters an antique look; it came up in the swearing episode as an alternative to a similar-sounding word.
Victorian printers' name for an exclamation mark.
Printers' slang for searching for scarce [[see:sorts]].
Said of the leather-covered inking balls when too much ink had been taken on them.
A name for a very small printing house.
Tweezers used to correct type.
Also called medial or swash s, an f-like letter without a crossbar in old books, the first half of [[see:eszett]].
German ligature literally meaning sz, whose first half is the [[see:long s]]; not needed in an English font.
A letter lost because European printers lacked it in their fonts; Rob wants it back to replace th everywhere.
Appears for 'the' because printers without a [[see:thorn]] used the similar-looking Y instead.
A letter Jess would like back alongside [[see:thorn]]; in modern Icelandic the two letters represent the two different th sounds.
From 1838 a drink and placeholder name; later typographic ornaments, a muffin, an insult, genitalia; a fool via [[see:The Dingbat Family]]; precursor to [[see:emoji]].
Typeface named after [[see:Hermann Zapf]]'s typographical ornaments, called [[from:dingbat]]s.
Used [[see:dingbat]] ornaments that became [[see:Zapf Dingbats]], and also created [[see:Optima]].
Comic strip by George Herriman probably behind the sense of [[see:dingbat]] as a foolish person, around 1905.
Show many Americans associate with the foolish-person sense of [[see:dingbat]].
From two Japanese words meaning picture and character; serendipitously similar to [[unrelated:emotion]] and [[unrelated:emote]], which helped it spread.
Looks and sounds similar to [[unrelated:emoji]] but is not related.
Looks and sounds similar to [[unrelated:emoji]] but is not related.
What we originally called such symbols; Rob assumed [[see:emoji]] was just a shortened form of it.
Typeface named after type designer [[from:Claude Garamond]].
Typeface named after [[from:John Baskerville]], an 18th-century printer and type designer.
Typeface named after [[from:William Caslon]], an English type founder.
Typeface named after an Italian printer.
Typeface named after a French dynasty of printers.
Typeface named for, and inspired by, the bold lettering of New York City signage.
Typeface named after the Latin name for Switzerland.
Named after a tabloid headline, 'Alien heads found in Georgia', because designer Matthew Carter liked the name's readability.
Typeface named after Egypt's capital because it was designed for Arabic script.
Typeface named after another typographer.
Typeface named after its Swiss creator.
A sans-serif typeface whose name reflects its modern, forward-looking aesthetic.
Named because it was created for the Times of London.
Typewriter-style typeface originally called [[see:Messenger]]; its inventor thought Courier fancier when handing it to IBM.
The original name of [[see:Courier]].
A humanist sans-serif by [[see:Hermann Zapf]], named for its balance and clarity.
A portmanteau of [[from:verdant]] and Ana, the name of the designer's daughter.
Typeface inspired by the lettering on [[from:Trajan's Column]] in Rome.
Typeface named for being high-impact.
